summary: What if the months-long journey to the far reaches of space were also a game in which you build your own colony? What would happen if we replaced overwhelming, tiresome medical tests and check-ups with an interactive system that rewards you for every task you complete in daily life on the station? In Nabu, every medical test you take and every workout you finish earns you coins, and those coins grow your very own base on the planet Nabu. On a long mission, the hardest part is taking care of yourself every single day, not just when something goes wrong. The astronaut plays, interacts and completes the tasks they are given, while the doctors and the psychologist receive exactly the data they need for the best possible monitoring. The app turns looking after your health into something the astronaut wants to do, not something they have to do. It doesn’t just watch over the astronaut; it teaches them to be their own doctor.
details:
We have developped an application called ‘Nabu’ that monitors aspects pertaining to the health and mental wellbeing of astronauts currently embarked on long space missions destined to reach Mars and other more distant objectives. It uses already existing data and incentivizes the recording of new data that can be used to efficaciously monitor and accurately display the physical, psychological, and cognitive status of the user. Our software stands out through the battery of medical tests and evaluations it can conduct.

The app can be used from two standpoints, one being the monitored astronaut’s and one being the monitoring psychologist’s. The astronaut inputs relevant data which the psychologist can then further analyze to determine their mental state and have the knowledge required to be able to provide all necessary aid. Logistically speaking, our prototype places the user in a game that takes place on a space colony located on a fictional planet, Nabu, named after the Babylonian god of wisdom and rational arts. Each astronaut has his own base which he is meant to maintain, develop, and customize using an in game currency called coins.

The core idea behind our project is motivating the users to accomplish their tasks by rewarding them for their completion with coins. These tasks include physical exercise, doing the integrated medical tests, as well as their usual tasks as astronauts that aren’t necessarily tied to their health, but to research and maintaining the travel module. These coins offer real life rewards such as the ability to make small decisions that can improve quality of life, such as choosing the wake-up music, picking the film on movie night, choosing what to eat for dinner on fridays, etc.(small inconveniences if you don’t have them, in order not to upset them or degrade their mental state any further, but things that still create enjoyment), as well as the ability to purchase in game furniture and other pieces of decoration to decorate their base, or unlock new modules in the fictional base which can be modified according to personal preference.

Nabu recognizes the movements of the joints and links them to certain exercises such as squats, bench presses, calf raises or deadlifts and documents the amount of repetitions and creates a graph that shows the intensity of said repetitions and their frequency. Other medical tests pertaining to cognition and physical health are based on official tests used by NASA.

The app asks for permission to use the device’s camera, which allows it to monitor ocular movement, and based on a pre-existing library of eye tracking recordings, it estimates how tired the astronaut is, another very important factor, given the majority of astronauts encounter problems with their sleep and rest at some point throughout the journey. The system measures how long the user keeps his eyes closed, as well as the position of their head, chest and shoulders. If there is an indication that the astronaut has fainted or is in a critical state, the app automatically sends out an alert in the form of a photo of his current state which will be visible in the psychologist’s dashboard.

The software also includes a dedicated journaling system, where users can write down their experiences, feelings and moods in a private manner. Knowing that this space is confidential and safe allows them to reset and regain their balance. The journal also has a built-in AI that detects passages and key words linked to the person’s overall mental state, without actually reading entire sentences, in order to maintain privacy.. When it finds signs of serious risk, it alerts their personal psychologist with a warning flag, without ever sending the journal text itself. There is also a public journal, where users can share their entries with other astronauts, acting as a sort of travel log. The personal journal and the community journal are kept completely separate.

In the main part of the station, which is unlocked from the start, the user has a room with a health console, living quarters, a bedroom and a mess hall, each designed to meet the main monitoring needs of the individual. As time passes and they collect more coins, they can unlock areas such as the greenhouse, which current NASA research shows is important for preventing psychological and cognitive decline, the observation lounge, the medical lab and more. The health console gives a summary of the user’s overall condition, made up of Vitals, Sleep & mind, Labs, Environment, a daily overview (“At a glance”) and a user guide (“Guidance”).

Unlike other monitoring apps, Nabu encourages users to record their data interactively, in a gamified and user-friendly way. People in the program get a virtual world that gives them something to strive for, which strengthens their ability to persevere throughout the mission. It is a safe space where they can find themselves again and freely share their physical, mental and cognitive state, as well as their feelings. The app is a virtual journey that runs alongside the real one, designed so that nothing that happens in the game affects the astronaut’s mind or situation in real life in a negative way.On a mission that seems to never end, the astronaut gets something very valuable: progress they can see with their own eyes. The colony grows every day, and that gives them a reason to keep going. Monotony and isolation are easier to bear when you are building and working on a project of your own, an active goal.

The app turns the tiring routine of logging medical data into a comfortable experience, instead of a chore people would rather avoid. The special part is that none of this feels like an obligation.

We hope to create a new, universal approach to astronaut health and well-being. Our goal is to show that taking care of your health in space can become an enjoyable habit, not a chore. In the long run, the same idea could also help people on Earth who live in isolation.
